archetype.name: Rebuilding (young and outshot)
archetype.definition: A team coming off a last-place finish that is giving big minutes to young players and is being outshot and outchanced most nights, so its record reflects real problems rather than bad breaks.

report.headline: Outchanced worse than last year's last-place team, and Lankinen's goaltending makes it uglier
report.take:
Vancouver finished 32nd of 32 on the site last season at 25-49-8. Eight games into this one it sits 29th at 2-6-0, and the underlying numbers are, if anything, worse. The Canucks own 40.6% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, 29th in the league, down from 44.2% a year ago. Their 44% shot-attempt share is 27th. This is not a decent team running into hot goalies. It spends most of its even-strength time defending.

Two things turn a bad possession team into a very bad record. The first is the goaltending split. Kevin Lankinen has started five games with a .786 save percentage and -10.8 goals saved above expected, 63rd of 64 goalies on the site. Leevi Merilainen has started three with a .926 and +2.1. The team's -8.7 GSAx ranks 31st, and Lankinen accounts for more than all of it. The second is the penalty kill, which has stopped only 57.1% of power plays, dead last. Those two problems explain why a middling offense (13th in goals per game, 3.25 a night) still sits next to the 31st-ranked defense and 4.75 goals allowed per game.

Some of the numbers flatter the team. A 99.9 PDO says the 5-on-5 percentages are roughly average, so there is no big bounce-back coming from luck at even strength. Paul Cotter has 4 goals on 8 shots with a 32.4% xGF, and that finishing will not hold. The -1.9 Pts vs Goal Diff (30th) does point to a little bad luck, with one-goal losses to Vegas and the Islanders, and that should even out somewhat. The bright spots are real but narrow. Elias Pettersson the center has 9 points and ranks 17th among 213 centers. Elias Pettersson the defenseman is 8th of 239 on the blue line with a 56.4% xGF and a +6, the only regular above water in chances. Meanwhile Zeev Buium plays 21.7 minutes a night with a 33.8% xGF, and that is the heart of a D+ blueline.

Where this goes depends mostly on the crease. If Merilainen takes the net, the Canucks should allow fewer goals and look like a below-average team rather than a disaster. The chance share, though, points to another season near the bottom of the Pacific. The current five-game losing streak and a road-heavy schedule against good teams make a quick climb unlikely.

strengths.title: Merilainen has stabilized the crease
strengths.body: In his three starts Leevi Merilainen has posted a .926 save percentage and positive GSAx, which ranks him 17th of 64 goalies. That is roughly average-to-good goaltending behind a team that allows a lot. It is a small sample, but it is the clearest lever the club can pull to cut its goals against right away.

strengths.title: Pettersson drives a middling offense
strengths.body: The offense ranks 13th in goals per game, respectable for a team this outshot. Center Elias Pettersson is the engine with 9 points, 4 of them on the power play. Filip Hronek adds 6 assists from the back end in nearly 25 minutes a night. The power play is about league average, and that output is repeatable. The depth scoring behind them is less so.

strengths.title: Pettersson (D) wins his minutes
strengths.body: Defenseman Elias Pettersson ranks 8th of 239 on his tab, owns a 56.4% xGF and is +6. That is the best on-ice profile on the roster by a distance. He plays only about 17 minutes. Giving him more of Buium's or Oleksiak's ice time is an obvious way to tilt the ice.

concerns.title: Outchanced worse than last season
concerns.body: A 40.6% xGF and 44% CF are both bottom-six marks. The xGF is below last year's 44.2%, when the team finished last on the site. Nearly every forward regular sits under 50% xGF, so this is a roster-wide possession problem, not a single bad line. With PDO near 100, there is no luck cushion hiding it, and it is the most likely trait to persist.

concerns.title: Lankinen and the penalty kill
concerns.body: Lankinen's .786 save percentage and -10.8 GSAx over five starts, combined with a league-worst 57.1% penalty kill, have turned close games into blowouts, as in the 7-9 loss to Edmonton and 2-7 at Carolina. The PK should rise toward normal as the save percentage behind it recovers. Whether that happens depends on who starts. If Lankinen keeps getting the net at this level, the defense will stay near the bottom.

concerns.title: Forwards run up points against
concerns.body: Opposing forwards are scoring 9.13 points a game against Vancouver, 2.41 above what their own averages predict. That ranks 30th, and centers fare best of all at 31st. Part of it is goaltending. Part of it is a blueline graded D+ that leans on Zeev Buium for 21.7 minutes with a 33.8% xGF. That deployment looks like development time, and it costs goals now.

trend.note: A competitive opening home stand gave way to a winless four-game road trip and a five-game losing streak, with October at 1-6. Scoring has also dipped to 2.86 goals a game in October.

weekAhead.headline: Florida, Tampa, then the league's top team: a brutal week
weekAhead.body:
The road trip runs on through Florida and Tampa before Carolina, the site's No. 1 team, comes to Vancouver a week after beating the Canucks 7-2. All three opponents rank in the top five in shot-attempt share. That is exactly the kind of team that pins a 44% CF club in its own end. Nothing here plays to Vancouver's strengths. A single win would be a reasonable week.

The softest spot is the Tampa game. The Lightning's power play is converting at 8.3%, 31st, which takes some pressure off the league's worst penalty kill. Tampa also gives up more than expected to defensemen, a small opening for Hronek and Pettersson from the back end. Florida's goaltending grades A-, so the Canucks' scoring will likely need the power play against a Panthers PK that ranks 23rd.

keyMatchups.title: Carolina's possession machine returns
keyMatchups.body: Carolina owns 59.5% of the expected goals and a 93.3% penalty kill, both second in the league. The Hurricanes already put seven past Vancouver. The Canucks' power play is unlikely to bail them out, so the game hinges on surviving 5-on-5.

keyMatchups.title: Tampa's dead power play
keyMatchups.body: Tampa's power play is 31st at 8.3%, the one matchup where Vancouver's 57.1% PK isn't a glaring liability. The Lightning still own 57.6% of 5-on-5 expected goals, though. Their shortfall is finishing and special teams, not territory.

keyMatchups.title: Florida's PK vs Vancouver's PP
keyMatchups.body: Florida grades A- in goal and controls 55% of shot attempts, but its penalty kill is only 75.9%. Vancouver's league-average power play, led by Pettersson and Boeser with 4 PP points each, is its best route to goals in Sunrise.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Merilainen gets the bulk of the starts over Lankinen: it is the single change that could keep these games close.

restOfSeason.body:
The possession numbers say this is a bottom-five team. That is not a fluke of eight games, because it continues last season's slide and is slightly worse. What should improve is the goaltending and the penalty kill that depends on it. Lankinen's start is extreme even for a struggling goalie, and Merilainen's early form suggests the crease can be league-average-ish. A small dose of close-game luck (-1.9 points vs goal differential) should also come back. Expect goals against to drift down from 4.75 a game toward the high threes.

What will not hold is the depth finishing, Cotter above all. And without a real jump in chance share, the offense's 13th-place standing is more likely to slip than climb. The realistic range is a team well out of the Pacific race, giving the young defensemen minutes and hoping the two Petterssons are the core of the next good team.
swingFactors: Penalty kill recovering toward league average
Young defensemen improving their chance share

confidence.note: Only eight games, but the possession numbers match last season's.
